title: Monarchy, Democracy and Dictatorship
bigQuestion: Who should hold power, and how can people tell whether they really choose their leaders?

story.title: Two Ballots on the Same Day
story.kicker: Two imagined countries vote on the same Sunday, and the ballots tell very different stories.
paragraphs: Imagine two countries holding elections on the same Sunday. In the first country, a woman named Lena walks to a school gym. She shows her name to a volunteer. She takes a paper ballot into a small booth with a curtain. Four names are printed on it, from four different parties.

Lena has watched the candidates argue on television for weeks. Newspapers have criticized every one of them. She marks her choice in private and drops the ballot in a box. That night, workers from several parties watch as the votes are counted. The leader in office loses, and she gives a speech thanking the winner.

In the second country, a man named Arman also goes to vote. His ballot has only one name. Next to it is a single box. There is a booth, but an official stands close by and watches who uses it. Posters of the one candidate cover the walls. No newspaper has printed a word against him.

The next day, the government announces that the candidate won almost every vote. Both countries held an election. Both can say that the people voted. But only one of them gave people a real choice. This chapter is about how to tell the difference.
story.think: Both countries held an election. What three details from the story show which election gave people a real choice?

lessons.title: Absolute Monarchy
lessons.mainIdea: In an absolute monarchy, one king or queen holds nearly all power and answers to no elected body.
reading: King Louis XIV of France ruled from 1643 to 1715, one of the longest reigns in European history. He built a huge palace at Versailles and made nobles live near him so he could watch them. He made war, set taxes and named officials largely as he chose.

This kind of government is called an *absolute monarchy*. A *monarch* is a king or queen who usually inherits the throne from a parent. In an absolute monarchy, the monarch's word is law. Many kings of that time said their right to rule came from God. This idea is called the divine right of kings.

Supporters said one strong ruler brought order and unity after years of civil war. Critics said no single person should have so much power, because no one could stop a ruler who made bad choices. A few countries today, such as Saudi Arabia, are still described as absolute monarchies.

words.d: a king or queen, who usually inherits the throne
a government in which the monarch holds nearly all power
the belief that a monarch's power comes from God

look.title: A Famous Line That May Not Be Real
look.text: Louis XIV is often quoted as saying, 'I am the state.' Many historians doubt he ever said it. The line first appears in books written long after his lifetime. Still, people keep repeating it because it seems to sum up how he ruled.
look.prompt: Why might a quotation spread even if no one can prove it was said? What should a careful reader do before repeating it?

check.q: What is a monarch?
choices: A king or queen who usually inherits the throne
check.why: The lesson defines a monarch as a king or queen who usually inherits the throne.

check.q: What did Louis XIV make nobles do?
check.why: The lesson says he made nobles live near him at Versailles so he could watch them.

check.q: Why do many historians doubt that Louis XIV said 'I am the state'?
choices: He said the opposite in a speech
It was carved on his palace
It first appears in books written long after his lifetime
check.why: The 'Look' says the line first appears in books written long after he lived.

lessons.title: Constitutional Monarchy
lessons.mainIdea: In a constitutional monarchy, the king or queen is head of state, but elected lawmakers make the laws.
reading: Britain went a different way. After years of struggle between kings and Parliament, the English Bill of Rights of 1689 limited the monarch. The king could not raise taxes or keep an army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. Over the next centuries, real power moved to elected lawmakers.

Today the United Kingdom is a *constitutional monarchy*. A *constitution* is the set of basic rules for a government. The king is the head of state and has an important role at public events. But the prime minister and Parliament make decisions, and the monarch stays out of party politics.

Japan, Spain, Sweden and Norway are also constitutional monarchies. Supporters say a monarch above politics can unite a country and link it to its history. Critics say no one should hold a public position just because of who their parents were. People in these countries still debate it.

words.d: the set of basic rules that says how a government works and what it may do
a government with a monarch whose powers are limited by a constitution and elected lawmakers

look.title: The English Bill of Rights, 1689
look.text: Levying money for or to the use of the Crown without grant of Parliament is illegal. Keeping a standing army in time of peace, unless with the consent of Parliament, is against law.
look.cite: English Bill of Rights, 1689 (wording shortened and modernized)
look.prompt: Which two powers does this passage take away from the monarch acting alone? Who must agree instead?

check.q: What is a constitution?
choices: The set of basic rules for a government
check.why: A constitution is the set of basic rules that says how a government works.

check.q: Under the English Bill of Rights, who had to agree before the Crown could raise money?
check.why: The Bill of Rights says levying money without grant of Parliament is illegal.

check.q: Which country is a constitutional monarchy today?
check.why: The lesson lists Japan, with the UK, Spain, Sweden and Norway, as constitutional monarchies.

lessons.title: Monarchs in Today's World
lessons.mainIdea: Only a small share of countries still have a monarch, and most of those monarchs have limited power.
reading: The United Nations has 193 member countries. Only about 43 of them have a monarch as head of state. That count includes 15 countries, such as Canada, Australia and Jamaica, that share King Charles III of the United Kingdom as their king.

Most of today's monarchies are constitutional. Their kings, queens and emperors open parliaments, greet visitors and stand for national unity. A smaller number, mostly in the Middle East, still give the monarch real control over government.
Most countries have no monarch at all. Many of them are *republics*. In a republic, the head of state is chosen, not born into the job. You will learn more about republics in the next section.

words.d: the person who officially stands for a country, such as a monarch or president
a country whose head of state is chosen rather than inheriting the position

look.title: Monarchs Among the World's Countries

look.cite: United Nations member list; counts of monarchies and Commonwealth realms as commonly reported (e.g., Encyclopaedia Britannica)
look.prompt: About what fraction of UN countries have a monarch? How many of the 43 share one king?

check.q: About how many countries have a monarch as head of state?
check.why: The lesson says about 43 of 193 UN countries have a monarch.

check.q: Which country shares King Charles III as its king?
check.why: Canada is one of the 15 countries that share King Charles III.

check.q: In a republic, the head of state is
choices: chosen rather than born into the job
check.why: A republic's head of state is chosen, not inherited.

lessons.title: Direct Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves instead of choosing others to do it.
reading: Around 500 BCE, the Greek city of Athens began one of the first *democracies*. The word comes from Greek words meaning 'the people rule.' Male citizens met on a hillside called the Pnyx. Thousands at a time listened to speeches and voted by raising their hands.

This is called *direct democracy*, because citizens decide laws themselves. But Athens left many people out. Women, enslaved people and foreigners living in the city could not vote. Only a minority of the people who lived there took part.

Direct democracy still exists in small places. In two Swiss cantons, or states, citizens meet outdoors once a year and vote by raising their hands. Many U.S. states, including Illinois, also let voters decide some questions directly on the ballot. Supporters say this is the purest form of self-rule. Critics say it is hard to run a big country this way.

words.d: government in which the people hold power, usually by voting
a democracy in which citizens vote on laws themselves
a full member of a country or city, with rights and duties

look.title: A Vote on the Hillside
look.text: Picture about six thousand men sitting on a rocky hill above Athens. A speaker climbs onto a stone platform and argues for building more warships. Another speaker argues against it. Then a leader calls for a vote, and a sea of hands goes up.
look.prompt: Who is on the hillside, and who is missing? How would the vote change if everyone living in Athens could take part?

check.q: What does 'democracy' come from?
check.why: The lesson says the word comes from Greek words meaning 'the people rule.'

check.q: Who could NOT vote in ancient Athens?
check.why: The reading says women, enslaved people and foreigners could not vote.

check.q: Which is an example of direct democracy today?
choices: A king naming a new prime minister
A general taking over a government
A party choosing a single candidate
Swiss citizens voting outdoors by raising their hands
check.why: In two Swiss cantons, citizens meet outdoors and vote directly on laws.

lessons.title: Representatives and Republics
lessons.mainIdea: In a representative democracy, people elect lawmakers to make decisions for them.
reading: The United States has more than 330 million people. They cannot all meet on a hill. So they elect *representatives*, people chosen to make laws for them. This is called representative democracy. Illinois voters, for example, elect members of the Illinois General Assembly in Springfield and members of Congress in Washington, D.C.

The United States is also a republic, because its president is elected, not born into power. France, Mexico and India are republics too. Each has an elected leader and elected lawmakers, though their systems differ in the details.

Most democracies today are representative. Supporters say representatives can study hard issues full time. Critics say representatives may drift away from what voters want. That is why regular elections matter: voters can keep a representative or replace one.

words.d: a person elected to make decisions and laws for a group of people
a democracy in which people elect lawmakers to decide for them

look.title: Who Checks Whom in Washington
look.cite: U.S. Constitution and federal law (House size set at 435 since 1913)
look.prompt: Which group is largest? Why might it help to have laws pass through more than one group of people?

check.q: What is a representative?
choices: A person elected to make laws for a group of people
check.why: A representative is chosen by voters to make decisions and laws for them.

check.q: Why is the United States called a republic?
choices: Its president is elected, not born into power
All citizens vote on every law
check.why: In a republic the head of state is chosen rather than inherited.

check.q: How many members does the U.S. House have?
check.why: The data shows the House has 435 members.

lessons.title: Checks and Balances
lessons.mainIdea: Checks and balances split power so that no one part of government can rule alone.
reading: Suppose Congress passes a law. The president can *veto* it, or refuse to sign it. Congress can still override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses. Later, the courts can decide whether the law follows the Constitution.

This system is called *checks and balances*. Power is split among three branches. The legislative branch makes laws. The executive branch carries them out. The judicial branch, the courts, decides what laws mean. Each branch can limit, or check, the others.

James Madison, one of the writers of the U.S. Constitution, explained the idea in 1788. People who hold power might misuse it, so power must be set against power. Many democracies divide power in some way. Critics note that checks can also make government slow, and some people see that slowness as a benefit.

words.d: a system in which each branch of government can limit the others
one of the main parts of a government: legislative, executive or judicial
the power to reject a law

look.title: Madison on Power
look.text: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. ... If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
look.prompt: What does Madison think about people who hold power? How do checks and balances follow from that idea?

check.q: Which branch of government makes laws?
check.why: The legislative branch, Congress, makes laws.

check.q: How can Congress pass a law after a president's veto?
choices: By a two-thirds vote in both houses
By holding a new election the same day
check.why: The reading says Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.

check.q: Madison wrote, 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.' What is his point?
choices: People are imperfect, so power needs limits
check.why: Madison meant that because people can misuse power, government must set power against power.

lessons.title: Free and Fair Elections
lessons.mainIdea: A free and fair election gives real choices, a secret vote, an honest count and a peaceful handover.
reading: Think back to Lena and Arman in the story. Both voted. But only Lena's vote could change who led her country. What made the difference? Political scientists look for a few clear signs.

First, there are real choices: more than one party can run and campaign. Second, the vote is a *secret ballot*, so no one can punish you for your choice. Third, the press is free to criticize any candidate. Fourth, the count is honest and watched by different sides.

The last sign is the most telling. A leader who loses must accept it and hand over power peacefully. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, says government should rest on the will of the people, shown in genuine elections.

words.d: a way of voting in private so no one knows or can punish your choice
an election with real choices, a secret vote, a free press and an honest count

look.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 21
look.text: The will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government; this will shall be expressed in periodic and genuine elections which shall be by universal and equal suffrage and shall be held by secret vote or by equivalent free voting procedures.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 21(3), 1948
look.prompt: Find two words in this passage that describe a fair election. Which one did Arman's election fail?

check.q: Why does a secret ballot matter?
choices: It lets the government know your vote
No one can punish you for your choice
check.why: A secret ballot keeps your choice private so no one can punish you.

check.q: Which sign does the lesson call the most telling?
choices: A high number of votes for one person
A losing leader handing over power peacefully
check.why: The lesson says the most telling sign is that a losing leader accepts it and hands over power.

check.q: According to Article 21, what should be the basis of a government's authority?
check.why: Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government.

lessons.title: One-Party States
lessons.mainIdea: In a one-party state, only one party may hold power, and other parties are banned or powerless.
reading: In the Soviet Union, from its early years until 1990, only the Communist Party was allowed to rule. Elections were held, but usually with one approved candidate for each seat. This is called a *one-party state*.

China today is a one-party state led by the Chinese Communist Party. Cuba, Vietnam and North Korea are also run by a single ruling party. Some of these states allow small, loyal parties to exist, but none of them may challenge the ruling party for power.

Supporters in these countries have argued that one party can plan for the long term and keep the nation united. Critics say that without rivals, a free press or fair votes, citizens cannot remove leaders who fail or abuse power. Human rights groups report jailing of critics in many one-party states.

words.d: a country where only one political party is allowed to hold power
an organized group that shares ideas and tries to win elections or power

look.title: The Ballot With One Name
look.text: Arman's ballot in the story had one name and one box. An official watched the booth. The government said the candidate won almost every vote.
look.prompt: Using this lesson, explain why the huge vote count does not prove the leader was popular. What else would you need to know?

check.q: Which country is described in the lesson as a one-party state today?
check.why: The lesson says China today is led by one party, the Chinese Communist Party.

check.q: What did elections in the Soviet Union usually offer?
choices: One approved candidate for each seat
check.why: The reading says Soviet elections usually had one approved candidate per seat.

check.q: What do critics say is the main problem with one-party states?
choices: Citizens cannot remove leaders who fail or abuse power
check.why: Without rivals or fair votes, citizens have no way to replace leaders.

lessons.title: Military Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Military rule happens when the armed forces take over and govern a country.
reading: On September 11, 1973, tanks rolled through Santiago, Chile. The army, led by General Augusto Pinochet, overthrew the elected president, Salvador Allende. This kind of sudden, forceful takeover is called a *coup*.

Pinochet's military government ruled until 1990. It closed Congress, banned parties and arrested thousands of opponents. Many were tortured or killed. Its supporters said it saved Chile from chaos and built a stronger economy. Chile returned to democracy after voters rejected Pinochet in a 1988 vote.

Chile is one example among many. Argentina, Greece, Myanmar and Nigeria have all had periods of *military rule*. Generals often promise order and quick fixes. Critics note that armies are trained to give orders, not to listen to voters, and that military rulers often hold on to power.

words.d: a sudden, often violent takeover of a government by a small group, often the army
government run by the armed forces instead of elected leaders

look.title: Two Promises
look.text: A general speaks on the radio: 'The country is in chaos. We have taken control to restore order. Elections will return when the time is right.' Fifteen years later, the same general is still in charge.
look.prompt: What did the general promise? What does the lesson say often happens to promises like this? Give the Chile example.

check.q: What is a coup?
choices: A sudden takeover of a government, often by the army
check.why: A coup is a sudden, forceful takeover of a government by a small group.

check.q: Who led the military government in Chile after 1973?
check.why: General Augusto Pinochet led the coup and ruled until 1990.

check.q: How did Chile return to democracy?
choices: Voters rejected Pinochet in a 1988 vote
check.why: The reading says Chile returned to democracy after voters rejected Pinochet in 1988.

lessons.title: Dictators of the 1900s
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1900s, dictators on both the far left and the far right took total control and caused enormous suffering.
reading: A *dictator* is a ruler who holds total power and cannot be removed by fair votes. The 1900s saw some of the most destructive dictators in history. Some came from the far left. Others came from the far right. You will study them in depth in later grades.

On the far left, Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until 1953. Millions died in his labor camps, called the Gulag, and in famines and purges. Mao Zedong ruled China from 1949 to 1976. Tens of millions died in the famine of his Great Leap Forward.

On the far right, Benito Mussolini ruled Italy from 1922 to 1943. Adolf Hitler ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945. His Nazi government murdered about six million Jews in the Holocaust, along with millions of others. Their ideas differed, but all four crushed free speech, banned rivals and used terror. This is why the two-line grid places them all near the authoritarian end.

words.d: a ruler with total power who cannot be removed by fair votes
the Nazi murder of about six million Jews, along with millions of others, during World War II

check.q: Which dictators came from the far right?
check.why: The lesson places Mussolini and Hitler on the far right, and Stalin and Mao on the far left.

choices: An absolute monarch holds nearly all power; a constitutional monarch's power is limited
A constitutional monarchy has no king or queen
review.why: Louis XIV held nearly all power, while in the UK today elected lawmakers make the laws.

review.q: Ancient Athens is best known as an early example of
review.why: Athenian citizens voted on laws themselves, which is direct democracy.
India has an elected head of state, so it is a republic.

review.q: The power of Congress to override a president's veto is an example of
review.why: Each branch can limit the others; an override checks the president.

choices: The army overthrew the elected president in a coup

choices: They had the same economic ideas
They were allies for their whole lives

review.why: Their economic ideas differed, but both ruled with total control, crushing speech and rivals.
